subproblem.title: A C^∞ chart has a C^∞ ambient left inverse near each of its points (inverse function theorem, Simon Ch. 2, 4.4; parent steps 4 and 6)
subproblem.statement: Ambient retraction onto the chart parameters. Data: P, d ∈ ℕ; M, W ⊆ ℝ^P; V ⊆ ℝ^d; ψ : ℝ^d → ℝ^P; v₀ ∈ ℝ^d. Hypotheses: V and W are open; ψ is C^∞ on V (ContDiffOn ℝ (⊤ : ℕ∞) ψ V) and injective on V; ψ(V) = W ∩ M; V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact for every compact K ⊆ W; Dψ(z) = fderiv ℝ ψ z is injective for every z ∈ V; v₀ ∈ V. Conclusion: there are an open set O ⊆ ℝ^P with ψ(v₀) ∈ O and a map ρ : ℝ^P → ℝ^d that is C^∞ on O, maps O into V, and satisfies ψ(ρ(z)) = z for every z ∈ M ∩ O.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P d : ℕ) (M W : Set (Euclid P)) (V : Set (Euclid d)) (ψ : Euclid d → Euclid P) (v₀ : Euclid d), IsOpen V → IsOpen W → ContDiffOn ℝ (⊤ : ℕ∞) ψ V → InjOn ψ V → ψ '' V = W ∩ M → (∀ K ⊆ W, IsCompact K → IsCompact (V ∩ ψ ⁻¹' K)) → (∀ z ∈ V, Injective (fderiv ℝ ψ z)) → v₀ ∈ V → ∃ (O : Set (Euclid P)) (ρ : Euclid P → Euclid d), IsOpen O ∧ ψ v₀ ∈ O ∧ ContDiffOn ℝ (⊤ : ℕ∞) ρ O ∧ MapsTo ρ O V ∧ ∀ z ∈ M ∩ O, ψ (ρ z) = z
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. Step 4 of the supplied proof of the parent ("As in Simon 4.4, the inverse function theorem (C^∞ version) applied to π_y∘(ψ − y) at ψ^{-1}(y), whose derivative π_y∘Dψ(ψ^{-1}(y)) is invertible …, gives an open ball D_y ⊆ ℝ^m centred at 0, an open set W_y ∋ y and a C^∞ map G_y : D_y → ℝ^P with M ∩ W_y = G_y(D_y) and π_y(G_y(a) − y) = a … [W_y exists because ψ is a homeomorphism of V onto W ∩ M: continuous, injective and proper.]") and the first part of its step 6 ("O_y := {z ∈ W_y : π_y(z − y) ∈ D_y}, an open set containing y … for z ∈ M ∩ O_y we have z ∈ M ∩ W_y = G_y(D_y), z = G_y(a) with a = π_y(z − y)"). Here ρ(z) := (π∘ψ)⁻¹(π(z)), so that ψ∘ρ is the parent's z ↦ G_y(π_y(z − y)) (the translation by y only shifts the target of π by the constant π(y)).

1. (ψ is a homeomorphism of V onto W ∩ M.) ψ is continuous on V (it is C^∞ there). Let C ⊆ V be relatively closed in V and let z ∈ W ∩ M be the limit of a sequence ψ(c_k) with c_k ∈ C. The set K := {z} ∪ {ψ(c_k) : k ∈ ℕ} is compact (a convergent sequence with its limit) and contained in W (ψ(c_k) ∈ ψ(V) = W ∩ M), so V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact and contains every c_k. Hence a subsequence c_{k_l} converges to some c ∈ V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) ⊆ V; c ∈ C because C is closed in V; and ψ(c) = lim ψ(c_{k_l}) = z by continuity of ψ at c ∈ V. Thus z ∈ ψ(C), i.e. ψ(C) is relatively closed in W ∩ M. Since ψ is a bijection of V onto W ∩ M, for every open S ⊆ V the set ψ(S) = (W ∩ M) ∖ ψ(V ∖ S) is relatively open in W ∩ M: ψ(S) = W₁ ∩ (W ∩ M) for some open W₁. Putting W₀ := W₁ ∩ W gives an open W₀ ⊆ W with ψ(S) = W₀ ∩ M.

2. (A left inverse of Dψ(v₀).) L₀ := Dψ(v₀) : ℝ^d → ℝ^P is injective, so there is a linear map π : ℝ^P → ℝ^d with π∘L₀ = id_{ℝ^d} (for instance π := (L₀*L₀)⁻¹L₀*, L₀*L₀ being invertible because L₀ is injective); π is continuous (finite dimension). The parent's choice π_y = ι_y* (ι_y a linear isometry of ℝ^d onto range L₀) serves equally: only the invertibility of π∘L₀ is used below.

3. (Inverse function theorem.) φ := π∘ψ is C^∞ on the open set V and Dφ(v₀) = π∘L₀ = id_{ℝ^d} is invertible. By the C^∞ inverse function theorem there is an open set S₀ ∋ v₀ that φ maps homeomorphically onto an open set T₀ ∋ φ(v₀). The set G := {z ∈ V : Dφ(z) is invertible} is open (z ↦ Dφ(z) is continuous on the open set V, and the invertible operators form an open subset of End(ℝ^d)) and contains v₀. Put S := S₀ ∩ G (⊆ V, open, v₀ ∈ S) and T := φ(S); T is open because φ|_{S₀} is a homeomorphism onto the open set T₀. So φ maps S homeomorphically onto T, with inverse φ⁻¹ : T → S, and Dφ is invertible at every point of S. At each t ∈ T, φ is C^∞ near φ⁻¹(t) with invertible derivative there, so by the inverse function theorem the local inverse φ⁻¹ is C^∞ near t. Hence φ⁻¹ is C^∞ on T. (A Lean route: ContDiffAt.hasStrictFDerivAt and HasStrictFDerivAt.toOpenPartialHomeomorph for S₀, T₀; ContinuousLinearEquiv.isOpen for the openness of G; OpenPartialHomeomorph.restrOpen to pass to S; OpenPartialHomeomorph.contDiffAt_symm for the smoothness of the inverse at each point of T.)

4. (O and ρ.) Apply step 1 to the open set S ⊆ V: there is an open W₀ ⊆ W with ψ(S) = W₀ ∩ M. Put O := W₀ ∩ π⁻¹(T), an open subset of ℝ^P, and ρ(z) := φ⁻¹(π(z)) for z ∈ O (and ρ(z) := v₀ for z ∉ O; values off the open set O play no role).
 - ψ(v₀) ∈ O: ψ(v₀) ∈ ψ(S) ⊆ W₀ and π(ψ(v₀)) = φ(v₀) ∈ T.
 - ρ is C^∞ on O: it is the composition of the continuous linear map π, which maps O into T, with φ⁻¹, which is C^∞ on T.
 - ρ maps O into S ⊆ V.
 - Let z ∈ M ∩ O. Then z ∈ W₀ ∩ M = ψ(S), so z = ψ(s) for some s ∈ S, and π(z) = φ(s). Hence ρ(z) = φ⁻¹(φ(s)) = s and ψ(ρ(z)) = ψ(s) = z.
 This proves the claim. ∎
proof_key_steps: Properness, continuity and injectivity make ψ a homeomorphism of V onto W ∩ M, so ψ(S) = W₀ ∩ M for every open S ⊆ V.
With π a linear left inverse of Dψ(v₀), φ = π∘ψ has Dφ(v₀) = id; the C^∞ inverse function theorem gives open S ∋ v₀, T = φ(S) and a C^∞ inverse φ⁻¹ : T → S.
O := W₀ ∩ π⁻¹(T) and ρ := φ⁻¹∘π satisfy ρ(O) ⊆ V and ψ(ρ(z)) = z for z ∈ M ∩ O.

subproblem.title: Generalized cross product of an (m+1)-dimensional subspace A₀ (the volume form of A₀, parent step 2)
subproblem.statement: Cross product in A₀. Data: P, m ∈ ℕ; a linear subspace A₀ ⊆ ℝ^P with dim A₀ = m + 1. Conclusion: there is a continuous alternating m-linear map N : (ℝ^P)^m → ℝ^P (an element of Euclid P [⋀^Fin m]→L[ℝ] Euclid P) such that for every w = (w_1, …, w_m) ∈ (ℝ^P)^m: (i) N(w) ∈ A₀; (ii) N(w)·w_j = 0 for every j; (iii) if (w_j) is orthonormal and every w_j ∈ A₀, then |N(w)| = 1; (iv) if (w_j) is linearly independent and every w_j ∈ A₀, then N(w) ≠ 0.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P m : ℕ) (A₀ : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P)), Module.finrank ℝ A₀ = m + 1 → ∃ N : Euclid P [⋀^Fin m]→L[ℝ] Euclid P, (∀ w : Fin m → Euclid P, N w ∈ A₀) ∧ (∀ (w : Fin m → Euclid P) (j : Fin m), inner ℝ (N w) (w j) = 0) ∧ (∀ w : Fin m → Euclid P, Orthonormal ℝ w → (∀ j, w j ∈ A₀) → ‖N w‖ = 1) ∧ ∀ w : Fin m → Euclid P, LinearIndependent ℝ w → (∀ j, w j ∈ A₀) → N w ≠ 0
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. Step 2 of the supplied proof of the parent ("Fix an orthonormal basis a_0, …, a_m of A₀ and let Ω(v_0, …, v_m) := det(a_i·v_j)_{i,j=0..m}, an alternating (m+1)-linear form on ℝ^P. Ω(v_0, …, v_m) = 0 if the v_j are linearly dependent or if some v_j is orthogonal to A₀; Ω(w_0, …, w_m) = ±1 for every orthonormal basis (w_j) of A₀ (the matrix (a_i·w_j) is orthogonal); Ω ≠ 0 on every basis of A₀"), together with the A₀-representative Σ_i Ω(…, a_i)a_i of the functional v ↦ Ω(…, v) used in its steps 3 and 5. The free vector slot of Ω is placed first here instead of last; this changes Ω(…) only by the sign (−1)^m, which is irrelevant for (i)–(iv).
Notation: the slots of Ω are indexed by 0, …, m; for u ∈ ℝ^P and w = (w_1, …, w_m) write (u, w) := (u, w_1, …, w_m) (Fin.cons u w). P_{A₀} denotes the orthogonal projection onto A₀.

1. (The volume form Ω.) Fix an orthonormal basis a_0, …, a_m of A₀ (it exists because dim A₀ = m + 1) and put Ω(v) := det(a_i·v_j)_{i,j=0..m} for v = (v_0, …, v_m) ∈ (ℝ^P)^{m+1}. Column j of the matrix depends linearly on v_j, so Ω is (m+1)-linear; if v_j = v_k for some j ≠ k, two columns coincide and Ω(v) = 0, so Ω is alternating. Since a_i·v_j = a_i·P_{A₀}(v_j), Ω(v) is unchanged if any v_j is replaced by P_{A₀}(v_j).

2. (Definition of N.) For w ∈ (ℝ^P)^m put N(w) := Σ_{i=0}^m Ω(a_i, w) a_i. For each fixed i, w ↦ Ω(a_i, w) is m-linear and alternating (step 1), so N is an alternating m-linear map ℝ^P × ⋯ × ℝ^P → ℝ^P. N is continuous: Ω(a_i, w) is the determinant of an (m+1)×(m+1) matrix whose entries a_k·a_i and a_k·w_j depend continuously (linearly) on w, and the determinant is a polynomial in the entries (Mathlib Continuous.matrix_det); so N is a continuous alternating map, i.e. N ∈ Euclid P [⋀^Fin m]→L[ℝ] Euclid P.

3. (Key identity.) For every u ∈ ℝ^P, N(w)·u = Ω(u, w). Indeed N(w)·u = Σ_i Ω(a_i, w)(a_i·u) = Ω(Σ_i (a_i·u)a_i, w) by linearity of Ω in slot 0, and Σ_i (a_i·u)a_i = P_{A₀}(u), so by step 1 this equals Ω(P_{A₀}(u), w) = Ω(u, w).

4. (i) N(w) is a linear combination of a_0, …, a_m ∈ A₀, hence N(w) ∈ A₀.

5. (ii) For j ∈ {1, …, m}, step 3 gives N(w)·w_j = Ω(w_j, w_1, …, w_m). The vector w_j occupies slot 0 and slot j, so this is 0 because Ω is alternating.

6. (The normal line of span w in A₀.) Suppose every w_j lies in A₀ and (w_1, …, w_m) is linearly independent; let S := span{w_1, …, w_m} ⊆ A₀, so dim S = m. The orthogonal complement of S inside A₀, A₀ ∩ S^⊥, has dimension (m + 1) − m = 1; let e be a unit vector in it. By (i), (ii) and linearity, N(w) ∈ A₀ and N(w) ⊥ S, so N(w) ∈ A₀ ∩ S^⊥ = ℝe, and N(w) = (N(w)·e)e = Ω(e, w)e by step 3. The family (e, w_1, …, w_m) is linearly independent (e ≠ 0 and e ⊥ S) and consists of m + 1 vectors of the (m+1)-dimensional space A₀, so it is a basis of A₀.

7. (iv) In the situation of step 6 let C := (a_i·(e, w)_j)_{i,j=0..m}. Every b ∈ A₀ equals Σ_i (a_i·b)a_i, so the columns of C are the coordinate vectors of the basis (e, w) of A₀ with respect to the basis (a_i); hence C is invertible and Ω(e, w) = det C ≠ 0. Therefore N(w) = Ω(e, w)e ≠ 0.

8. (iii) If (w_j) is orthonormal and every w_j ∈ A₀, it is linearly independent, so step 6 applies, and now (e, w_1, …, w_m) is an orthonormal basis of A₀. For b, b' ∈ A₀, Parseval's identity in the orthonormal basis (a_i) gives b·b' = Σ_i (a_i·b)(a_i·b'); so the columns of C are orthonormal in ℝ^{m+1}, CᵀC = I and det C = ±1. Hence |N(w)| = |Ω(e, w)|·|e| = |det C| = 1. ∎
proof_key_steps: Ω(v_0, …, v_m) := det(a_i·v_j) for an orthonormal basis (a_i) of A₀ is alternating and sees only the A₀-components of its arguments.
N(w) := Σ_i Ω(a_i, w)a_i is a continuous alternating map with N(w)·u = Ω(u, w) for all u.
Hence N(w) ∈ A₀ and N(w)·w_j = Ω(w_j, w) = 0 (repeated argument).
For independent w in A₀, N(w) = Ω(e, w)e with e the unit normal of span w in A₀; Ω(e, w) is the determinant of a change of basis, nonzero, and ±1 when w is orthonormal.

audit.reason: The determinant construction gives a continuous alternating map and the identity inner(N(w), u) = Ω(u, w). This proves orthogonality for arbitrary w; the normal-line and determinant arguments prove nonvanishing and unit norm under their respective hypotheses.

subproblem.statement: Hyperplane projection in A₀. Data: P, m ∈ ℕ; linear subspaces A₀, Q ⊆ ℝ^P; n ∈ ℝ^P. Hypotheses: dim A₀ = m + 1; dim Q = m; Q ⊆ A₀; n ∈ A₀; |n| = 1; n·v = 0 for every v ∈ Q. Step 1 of the supplied proof of the parent ("Hence N_x := A₀ ∩ T_x^⊥ is a line and A₀ = T_x ⊕ N_x orthogonally"), used in its step 3 ("ν₀(x) ∈ N_x and ν₀(x) = λn") and, as the identity P_x = P_{A₀} − ν(x)⊗ν(x), to obtain the continuity of x ↦ P_x in (7a). Stated here for an abstract m-dimensional subspace Q ⊆ A₀ (in the parent Q = span T_x) and unit normal n.

1. (Q is the orthogonal complement of n inside A₀.) Since n ∈ A₀ and n ≠ 0 (|n| = 1), the line ℝn is a 1-dimensional subspace of A₀, and the orthogonal complement of ℝn inside A₀, A₀ ∩ n^⊥, has dimension (m + 1) − 1 = m. Every v ∈ Q lies in A₀ (Q ⊆ A₀) and satisfies n·v = 0, so Q ⊆ A₀ ∩ n^⊥. Both spaces have dimension m, hence Q = A₀ ∩ n^⊥.

2. (The candidate.) Fix w ∈ ℝ^P and put u := P_{A₀}w − (n·w)n. Then u ∈ A₀, because P_{A₀}w ∈ A₀ and n ∈ A₀. Moreover n·u = n·P_{A₀}w − (n·w)|n|² = (P_{A₀}n)·w − n·w = 0, since P_{A₀} is self-adjoint, P_{A₀}n = n (n ∈ A₀) and |n| = 1. By step 1, u ∈ Q.

3. (Orthogonality of the remainder.) w − u = (w − P_{A₀}w) + (n·w)n. For v ∈ Q we have v ∈ A₀, so (w − P_{A₀}w)·v = 0 (w − P_{A₀}w is orthogonal to A₀), and n·v = 0 by hypothesis. Hence (w − u)·v = 0 for every v ∈ Q.

4. (Conclusion.) The orthogonal projection P_Q w is the unique u ∈ Q with w − u orthogonal to Q (characterization of the orthogonal projection, Mathlib Submodule.eq_starProjection_of_mem_of_inner_eq_zero). By steps 2 and 3, P_Q w = u = P_{A₀}w − (n·w)n. ∎

Remark (how the siblings use it). If u ∈ A₀ is orthogonal to Q, then P_Q u = 0 and P_{A₀}u = u, so the identity gives u = (n·u)n: every vector of A₀ orthogonal to Q is a multiple of n.

w − u = (w − P_{A₀}w) + (n·w)n is orthogonal to Q, so u = P_Q w.

subproblem.title: Local C^∞ extensions glue to a C^∞ extension on an open neighbourhood (smooth partition of unity, parent step 6)
subproblem.statement: Gluing local smooth extensions. Data: P ∈ ℕ; a real normed space F; M ⊆ ℝ^P; f : ℝ^P → F. Hypothesis: every y ∈ M has an open set O_y ∋ y and a map g_y : ℝ^P → F that is C^∞ on O_y (ContDiffOn ℝ (⊤ : ℕ∞) g_y O_y) with g_y(z) = f(z) for every z ∈ M ∩ O_y. Conclusion: there are ν : ℝ^P → F and an open set O ⊆ ℝ^P with M ⊆ O such that ν is C^∞ on O and ν(x) = f(x) for every x ∈ M.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (F : Type) [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F] (M : Set (Euclid P)) (f : Euclid P → F), (∀ y ∈ M, ∃ (O : Set (Euclid P)) (g : Euclid P → F), IsOpen O ∧ y ∈ O ∧ ContDiffOn ℝ (⊤ : ℕ∞) g O ∧ ∀ z ∈ M ∩ O, g z = f z) → ∃ (ν : Euclid P → F) (O : Set (Euclid P)), IsOpen O ∧ M ⊆ O ∧ ContDiffOn ℝ (⊤ : ℕ∞) ν O ∧ ∀ x ∈ M, ν x = f x
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. Step 6 of the supplied proof of the parent: "O := ⋃_{y∈M} O_y is open and contains M. As an open subset of ℝ^P it is a σ-compact smooth manifold, so there is a smooth partition of unity (λ_i)_{i∈I} on O subordinate to the open cover {O_y} (Mathlib SmoothPartitionOfUnity.exists_isSubordinate): λ_i ∈ C^∞(O; [0, 1]), tsupport λ_i ⊆ O_{y(i)} (closure in O), the family is locally finite, and Σ_iλ_i = 1 on O. Define ν(z) := Σ_iλ_i(z)ν_{y(i)}(z) for z ∈ O, each term being C^∞ on O …, the sum being locally finite; and ν(z) := 0 for z ∉ O. Then ν is C^∞ on O, and for x ∈ M, ν(x) = Σ_iλ_i(x)ν₀(x) = ν₀(x)." Here the local extensions g_y are arbitrary (in the parent g_y = ν_y and f = ν₀) and the codomain is any real normed space F.

1. (The open set.) For each y ∈ M choose O_y and g_y as in the hypothesis and put O := ⋃_{y∈M} O_y. O is open, and M ⊆ O because y ∈ O_y.

2. (O as a manifold.) Regard O as an open submanifold of ℝ^P: its charts are the restrictions of the identity chart of ℝ^P (model space ℝ^P with the trivial model with corners), so O is a C^∞ manifold. O is Hausdorff and second countable (a subspace of ℝ^P) and locally compact (an open subset of the locally compact space ℝ^P; in Lean via the open embedding of the subtype, IsOpenEmbedding.locallyCompactSpace); hence O is σ-compact (a locally compact second-countable space is σ-compact). Therefore smooth partitions of unity on O subordinate to any open cover of O exist (Mathlib SmoothPartitionOfUnity.exists_isSubordinate, applied to the closed subset O of the manifold O).

3. (Partition of unity.) The sets O_y (y ∈ M) form an open cover of O. Let (λ_i)_{i∈I} be a smooth partition of unity on O subordinate to it: each λ_i : O → [0, 1] is C^∞, the family of supports is locally finite, Σ_i λ_i = 1 on O, and for each i there is y(i) ∈ M with tsupport λ_i ⊆ O_{y(i)} (closure taken in O).

4. (The glued map.) For p ∈ O put G(p) := Σ_i λ_i(p)·g_{y(i)}(p), a finite sum near every point by local finiteness. Each term λ_i·g_{y(i)} is C^∞ on O: near a point of the open set O_{y(i)} it is a product of C^∞ functions, and a point of O ∖ O_{y(i)} lies outside the set tsupport λ_i, which is closed in O, so the term vanishes on a neighbourhood of it. A locally finite sum of C^∞ functions is C^∞, so G is C^∞ on O.

5. (G = f on M.) Let x ∈ M. If λ_i(x) ≠ 0 then x ∈ tsupport λ_i ⊆ O_{y(i)}, so x ∈ M ∩ O_{y(i)} and g_{y(i)}(x) = f(x). Hence G(x) = Σ_i λ_i(x)·f(x) = f(x).
 (Equivalently, steps 3–5 are Mathlib's local-to-global theorem for convex constraints, exists_contMDiffMap_forall_mem_convex_of_local, on the manifold O with t(p) := {f(p)} for p ∈ M and t(p) := F for p ∉ M — all convex: for p ∈ O pick y with p ∈ O_y; then O_y ∩ O is a neighbourhood of p in O on which g_y is C^∞, and g_y(q) ∈ t(q) for every q in it.)

6. (Back to ℝ^P.) Define ν(z) := G(z) for z ∈ O and ν(z) := 0 for z ∉ O. Since O is open in ℝ^P and the charts of O are restrictions of the identity of ℝ^P, smoothness of G at a point p of the manifold O is the same as smoothness of ν at p in ℝ^P (Mathlib contMDiffAt_subtype_iff together with contMDiffAt_iff_contDiffAt; ν restricted to O is G). So ν is C^∞ at every point of the open set O, i.e. ν is C^∞ on O, and ν(x) = G(x) = f(x) for every x ∈ M ⊆ O. ∎

A smooth partition of unity (λ_i) on O subordinate to {O_y} gives G := Σ_i λ_i g_{y(i)}, C^∞ on O.
At x ∈ M every nonzero term has g_{y(i)}(x) = f(x), so G(x) = f(x); extending G by 0 off O gives ν, C^∞ on O.

subproblem.title: The orientation of a hypersurface of A₀ defines a continuous unit normal in A₀ (parent step 3)
subproblem.statement: Continuous unit normal from an orientation. Data: P, m ∈ ℕ; a linear subspace A₀ ⊆ ℝ^P with dim A₀ = m + 1; M ⊆ ℝ^P; ξ : ℝ^P → Λ_m(ℝ^P) (MultiVector P m, the dual of the m-covectors). Hypotheses: tangentSpace M x ⊆ A₀ for every x ∈ M; ξ is an orientation of M (IsOrientation m M ξ: ξ is continuous on M, and for every x ∈ M there are a linear subspace Q with underlying set tangentSpace M x and an orthonormal family τ = (τ_1, …, τ_m) spanning Q such that ξ(x)(α) = α(τ) for every m-covector α, or ξ(x)(α) = −α(τ) for every α). Conclusion: there is ν₀ : ℝ^P → ℝ^P, continuous on M, such that for every x ∈ M: ν₀(x) ∈ A₀, |ν₀(x)| = 1 and ν₀(x)·v = 0 for every v ∈ tangentSpace M x.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P m : ℕ) (A₀ : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P)) (M : Set (Euclid P)) (ξ : Euclid P → MultiVector P m), Module.finrank ℝ A₀ = m + 1 → (∀ x ∈ M, tangentSpace M x ⊆ (A₀ : Set (Euclid P))) → IsOrientation m M ξ → ∃ ν₀ : Euclid P → Euclid P, ContinuousOn ν₀ M ∧ ∀ x ∈ M, ν₀ x ∈ A₀ ∧ ‖ν₀ x‖ = 1 ∧ ∀ v ∈ tangentSpace M x, inner ℝ (ν₀ x) v = 0
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. Step 3 of the supplied proof of the parent ("By IsOrientation, ξ(x) is a unit orientation of T_x: there are an orthonormal basis τ_1, …, τ_m of T_x and ε_x ∈ {1, −1} with ξ(x)(β) = ε_x·β(τ_1, …, τ_m) for every m-covector β. Put ℓ_x(v) := ξ(x)(ι_vΩ) … Define ν₀(x) := Σ_{i=0}^m ℓ_x(a_i)a_i ∈ A₀ … thus |ν₀(x)| = 1. Since ν₀(x) = Σ_i ξ(x)(ι_{a_i}Ω)a_i and ξ is continuous on M, ν₀ is continuous on M"). The volume form Ω of A₀ and the A₀-representatives of the functionals v ↦ Ω(…, v) are packaged in the sibling lemma cross_product (Submission.codim1_hcp_un_cross_product), and the components of ν₀ are read off in the standard basis of ℝ^P instead of the basis (a_i) of A₀; up to the irrelevant sign (−1)^m this is the same vector.

1. (The cross product.) By cross_product (dim A₀ = m + 1) fix a continuous alternating m-linear map N : (ℝ^P)^m → ℝ^P such that for every w ∈ (ℝ^P)^m: N(w) ∈ A₀; N(w)·w_j = 0 for every j; and |N(w)| = 1 whenever (w_j) is orthonormal with every w_j ∈ A₀.

2. (Covectors.) Let e_1, …, e_P be the standard basis of ℝ^P. For k = 1, …, P let β_k be the m-covector w ↦ e_k·N(w): the composition of the continuous alternating map N with the continuous linear functional u ↦ e_k·u, hence continuous, m-linear and alternating, i.e. β_k ∈ Covector (Euclid P) m.

3. (Definition and continuity of ν₀.) Put ν₀(x) := Σ_{k=1}^P ξ(x)(β_k) e_k for x ∈ ℝ^P. The map Λ : Λ_m(ℝ^P) → ℝ^P, Λ(η) := Σ_k η(β_k)e_k, is linear and continuous (each η ↦ η(β_k) is evaluation of a continuous linear functional at the fixed covector β_k), and ν₀ = Λ∘ξ. Since ξ is continuous on M (IsOrientation), ν₀ is continuous on M.

4. (ν₀ = ±N(τ) on M.) Let x ∈ M. By IsOrientation there are a subspace Q with underlying set tangentSpace M x, an orthonormal family τ = (τ_1, …, τ_m) with span{τ_1, …, τ_m} = Q, and ε ∈ {1, −1} with ξ(x)(α) = ε·α(τ) for every m-covector α. Taking α = β_k gives ξ(x)(β_k) = ε·(e_k·N(τ)), so ν₀(x) = Σ_k ε(e_k·N(τ))e_k = ε·N(τ).

5. (Properties at x ∈ M.) Each τ_j lies in Q, whose underlying set is tangentSpace M x ⊆ A₀. By step 1:
 - N(τ) ∈ A₀, so ν₀(x) = εN(τ) ∈ A₀;
 - τ is orthonormal with every τ_j ∈ A₀, so |ν₀(x)| = |N(τ)| = 1;
 - every v ∈ tangentSpace M x lies in Q = span{τ_j}, say v = Σ_j c_jτ_j, so ν₀(x)·v = ε Σ_j c_j (N(τ)·τ_j) = 0.
 Together with step 3 this proves the claim. ∎
proof_key_steps: Take the cross product N of A₀ (cross_product) and the covectors β_k := e_k·N(·).
ν₀ := Σ_k ξ(·)(β_k)e_k is a continuous linear image of ξ, hence continuous on M.
At x ∈ M, ξ(x) = ±τ_1∧⋯∧τ_m gives ν₀(x) = ±N(τ): a unit vector of A₀ orthogonal to span τ = tangentSpace M x.

audit.reason: Evaluation on fixed covectors constructs a continuous linear image of ξ. The orientation hypothesis supplies one consistent sign per point, giving ν₀ = ±N(τ) and all required properties. No unstated embeddedness assumption is used.

subproblem.title: Tangent spaces of an embedded C¹ submanifold contained in a subspace A₀ are m-dimensional subspaces of A₀ (parent step 1)
subproblem.statement: Tangent spaces lie in A₀. Data: P, m ∈ ℕ; a linear subspace A₀ ⊆ ℝ^P; M ⊆ ℝ^P. Hypotheses: M is an embedded C¹ m-dimensional submanifold of ℝ^P (IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m M: every y ∈ M has open V ⊆ ℝ^m, open W ∋ y and ψ : ℝ^m → ℝ^P, C¹ and injective on V, with ψ(V) = W ∩ M, V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) compact for compact K ⊆ W, and Dψ(z) injective for z ∈ V) and M ⊆ A₀. Conclusion: for every x ∈ M there is a linear subspace Q ⊆ ℝ^P whose underlying set is tangentSpace M x = {γ'(0) : γ C¹ on (−1, 1), γ((−1, 1)) ⊆ M, γ(0) = x}, with dim Q = m and Q ⊆ A₀.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P m : ℕ) (A₀ : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P)) (M : Set (Euclid P)), IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m M → M ⊆ (A₀ : Set (Euclid P)) → ∀ x ∈ M, ∃ Q : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P), (Q : Set (Euclid P)) = tangentSpace M x ∧ Module.finrank ℝ Q = m ∧ Q ≤ A₀
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. Step 1 of the supplied proof of the parent (codim1_hcp_minimal_unit_normal): "T_x := tangentSpace M x is an m-dimensional linear subspace (chart_tangent_space) and T_x ⊆ A₀: if v = γ'(0) for a C¹ curve γ with values in M ⊆ A₀, then v = lim_{s→0}(γ(s) − γ(0))/s lies in the closed subspace A₀." Sibling lemma: chart_tangent_space (Submission.chart_tangentSpace_eq_range_fderiv).

1. (A chart at x.) Let x ∈ M. By IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m M there are open sets V ⊆ ℝ^m and W ⊆ ℝ^P with x ∈ W and a map ψ : ℝ^m → ℝ^P that is C¹ on V and injective on V, with ψ(V) = W ∩ M, V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) compact for every compact K ⊆ W, and Dψ(z) = fderiv ℝ ψ z injective for every z ∈ V. Since x ∈ W ∩ M = ψ(V), pick v ∈ V with ψ(v) = x.

2. (The subspace Q.) Let L := Dψ(v) : ℝ^m → ℝ^P and let Q := range L, a linear subspace of ℝ^P (the range of a linear map; its underlying set is Set.range L). By chart_tangent_space, applied with d = m, r = 1, its set argument taken to be M, and the chart (V, W, ψ) of step 1 (its hypotheses are exactly 1 ≤ 1 and the chart properties of step 1, together with v ∈ V), tangentSpace M (ψ(v)) = range L. As ψ(v) = x, the underlying set of Q is tangentSpace M x.

3. (Dimension.) L is injective, so it maps ℝ^m isomorphically onto Q, and dim Q = dim ℝ^m = m (rank–nullity).

4. (Q ⊆ A₀.) Let w ∈ Q = tangentSpace M x. By the definition of tangentSpace there is γ : ℝ → ℝ^P, C¹ on (−1, 1), with γ(s) ∈ M for every s ∈ (−1, 1), γ(0) = x, and γ'(0) = w (HasDerivAt γ w 0). For 0 < |s| < 1 the points γ(s) and γ(0) lie in M ⊆ A₀, so the difference quotient q(s) := s⁻¹(γ(s) − γ(0)) lies in the linear subspace A₀. Since γ has derivative w at 0, q(s) → w as s → 0 with s ≠ 0 (characterization of the derivative by difference quotients along the punctured neighbourhood filter of 0, which is nontrivial). A₀ is a linear subspace of the finite-dimensional space ℝ^P, hence closed, and q(s) ∈ A₀ for all s in the punctured neighbourhood (−1, 1) ∖ {0} of 0. Therefore the limit w lies in A₀.

5. Hence Q is a linear subspace with underlying set tangentSpace M x, dim Q = m and Q ⊆ A₀. ∎
proof_key_steps: A C¹ chart ψ with ψ(v) = x and chart_tangent_space give tangentSpace M x = range Dψ(v) =: Q.
Dψ(v) is injective on ℝ^m, so dim Q = m.
Difference quotients of a C¹ curve in M ⊆ A₀ lie in the closed subspace A₀, so γ'(0) ∈ A₀; hence Q ⊆ A₀.

audit.reason: The declared chart dependency identifies the tangent set with an injective derivative's range, giving dimension m. Curve difference quotients lie in the closed subspace A₀, proving containment without additional hypotheses.

subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. Step 7 of the supplied proof of the parent ((7a) continuity of div_M ν on M; (7b) stationarity tested with X = φν gives ∫_M φ·div_M ν dH^m = 0; (7c) continuity and positivity of H^m on small balls force div_M ν ≡ 0), with (7c) packaged in the sibling fundamental_lemma (Submission.codim1_hcp_un_fundamental_lemma). Departure in (7a): continuity of x ↦ P_x on M is obtained from the hypersurface identity P_x = P_{A₀} − ν(x)⊗ν(x) (step 2 below, the sibling hyperplane_projection) instead of the chart formula P_x = DG_y(a)(DG_y(a)*DG_y(a))^{-1}DG_y(a)*; it needs only the continuity of ν. Sibling lemmas: tangent_subspace (Submission.codim1_hcp_un_tangent_subspace), hyperplane_projection (Submission.codim1_hcp_un_hyperplane_projection), fundamental_lemma, density_one (Submission.dimred_rpd_submanifold_density_one), locally_closed (Submission.dimred_rpd_embedded_locally_closed).
Notation: H^m := μHE[m]; for x ∈ M, T_x := tangentSpace M x and P_x := the orthogonal projection onto span T_x; P_{A₀} := the orthogonal projection onto A₀; h(x) := trace(P_x∘Dν(x)) for x ∈ ℝ^P (P_x defined by the same formula for every x); O is an open set with M ⊆ O on which ν is C^∞.

1. (Tangent spaces.) For x ∈ M, tangent_subspace (IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m M and M ⊆ A₀) gives a subspace Q_x with underlying set T_x, dim Q_x = m and Q_x ⊆ A₀. Hence span T_x = Q_x and P_x is the orthogonal projection onto Q_x.

2. (Projection formula.) Let x ∈ M. Then P_x w = P_{A₀}w − (ν(x)·w)ν(x) for every w ∈ ℝ^P: apply hyperplane_projection with Q := Q_x (dim m, Q_x ⊆ A₀, step 1), dim A₀ = m + 1 and n := ν(x), which lies in A₀, has |ν(x)| = 1 and is orthogonal to every v ∈ Q_x = T_x (hypotheses).

3. (Continuity of h on M.) For z ∈ ℝ^P put F(z) := trace(P_{A₀}∘Dν(z)) − ν(z)·Dν(z)ν(z). For x ∈ M, step 2 gives P_x∘Dν(x) = P_{A₀}∘Dν(x) − R_x, where R_x w := (ν(x)·Dν(x)w)ν(x) is a rank-one map whose trace is ν(x)·Dν(x)ν(x); hence h(x) = F(x). F is continuous on O: ν is C^∞ on the open set O, so ν and z ↦ Dν(z) are continuous on O, and composition with P_{A₀}, the trace and the inner product are continuous (finite dimension). As M ⊆ O and h = F on M, h is continuous on M.

4. (Test fields.) Put U' := O ∩ U, an open set containing M. Let φ : ℝ^P → ℝ be C^∞ with compact support and tsupport φ ⊆ U', and define X(z) := φ(z)ν(z).
 (a) X is C^∞ on ℝ^P, in particular C¹: near every point of the open set O, X is a product of C^∞ functions; a point z ∉ O lies outside the closed set tsupport φ ⊆ O, so φ, and hence X, vanishes on a neighbourhood of z.
 (b) X vanishes wherever φ does, so tsupport X ⊆ tsupport φ, which is compact and contained in U' ⊆ U. Thus X has compact support and tsupport X ⊆ U.
 (c) For x ∈ M ⊆ O the product rule gives DX(x)w = φ(x)Dν(x)w + (Dφ(x)w)ν(x). The trace is linear and the rank-one map w ↦ ℓ(w)u has trace ℓ(u), so trace(P_x∘DX(x)) = φ(x)h(x) + Dφ(x)(P_xν(x)) = φ(x)h(x), because ν(x) ⊥ T_x gives ν(x) ⊥ span T_x and P_xν(x) = 0.
 (d) By stationarity applied to X (admissible by (a) and (b)), ∫_M trace(P_x∘DX(x)) dH^m(x) = 0. By (c) the integrand equals φ(x)h(x) at every x ∈ M (and M is measurable, step 5), so ∫_M φ·h dH^m = 0.

5. (Measurability, finiteness, positivity.) By locally_closed, M is measurable. For every compact K ⊆ U' we have K ⊆ U, so H^m(M ∩ K) < ∞ by hypothesis. For x ∈ M and s > 0, H^m(M ∩ B_s(x)) > 0: by density_one (IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m M, x ∈ M), H^m(M ∩ B_t(x))/(ω_m t^m) → 1 as t ↓ 0, where ω_m = unitBallVolume m; if H^m(M ∩ B_s(x)) were 0, then H^m(M ∩ B_t(x)) = 0 for every t ∈ (0, s] by monotonicity, so the quotient would be 0 for all these t, contradicting the limit 1.

6. (Conclusion.) Apply fundamental_lemma with the measure H^m, the open set U', the set M ⊆ U' and the function h: M is measurable, h is continuous on M (step 3), H^m(M ∩ K) < ∞ for every compact K ⊆ U' and H^m(M ∩ B_s(x)) > 0 for x ∈ M, s > 0 (step 5), and ∫_M φ·h dH^m = 0 for every C^∞ φ with compact support and tsupport φ ⊆ U' (step 4). Hence h(x) = trace(P_x∘Dν(x)) = 0 for every x ∈ M. ∎
